La Raya Pass lies on the road between Cusco and Puno and marks the transition between two regions. Here, the route opens onto a sweeping high-altitude landscape: pastures, a broad valley and mountain ranges form a panorama of the Andean plateau.

La Raya is a natural stop during the drive. Unlike the urban and archaeological stops along the route, the focus here is on the Andes themselves. On a clear day, distant peaks are easy to see, while shifting clouds emphasize the scale of the mountain valley.

La Unión lies in eastern El Salvador on the Gulf of Fonseca. It features in Central American itineraries as a place to leave the road and continue across the water. Its coastal setting shapes much of the local scenery.

Nearby, the gulf's islands and views from Conchagua Volcano are among the highlights. Visiting La Unión reveals another side of El Salvador, where the city, the sea and neighboring countries all lie close together. A stop here adds the region's maritime geography to a journey and gives you time to take in the coast before continuing on.

At Lagartococha, the Ecuadorian Amazon is best explored by canoe. The lake and surrounding wetlands are part of the nature routes around Sacha Lodge near the Napo River. It is hard to tell where the water ends and the forest begins: trunks are reflected in the dark surface, roots reach toward the shore, and another stretch of greenery appears around each bend.

Moving slowly by boat gives you time to notice the details. You can watch a bird above the water, trace the tangle of branches, or listen as the sounds of the forest change. A local guide reads these signs much more quickly and helps spot wildlife. Caimans and other inhabitants of Amazonian wetlands live here, although every sighting depends on the conditions of that particular outing.

Lagartococha is particularly appealing to visitors who want to combine a forest experience with time on the water. Channels and access points change with water levels, so the route is chosen on the spot. It is the kind of place where you want to put your phone away, pick up binoculars, and focus on what appears right beside the canoe.

### Atitlán — Guatemala's most beautiful lake

Atitlán is poetically interpreted as “the place where the rainbow gets its colors.” Strikingly beautiful and considered one of the world's loveliest lakes, Lake Atitlán lies in the crater of an extinct volcano, amid basalt slopes covered with tropical vegetation, and draws travelers from around the world.

Maya communities live along the lake's shores. They continue to preserve their traditions, speak their own languages and wear traditional clothing of the kind more commonly seen in museums or at festivals in large cities. Visitors come to discover Indigenous life, enjoy the scenery and find quiet. The area is also nicknamed Gringotenango (“place of foreigners”).

## Visiting the Lake Atitlán area

### Towns around Atitlán

Several small towns lie around the lake. Panajachel, on the northeastern shore, has many hotels, cafés, shops, activities and excursions. San Pedro La Laguna, on the western shore, attracts mostly backpackers. It is less tourist-oriented but still comfortable for a stay. San Marcos La Laguna, a little farther north, is the quietest of the three.
